Douglas Indian Association

Douglas Indian Association’s public history places its roots with T’aaḵu Kwáan and A’akw Kwáan families in the Juneau–Douglas region of Southeast Alaska. Its history booklet and environmental program page offer a community-directed path from displacement and renewed organizing to present-day stewardship priorities.

Start reading here

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Regional roots and named community places

The Tribal History booklet describes connections with T’aaḵu Kwáan and A’akw Kwáan families and with both Juneau and Douglas Indian Villages. Its account places Mayflower Island across from Douglas Indian Village and recalls the community’s effort to secure a school for children through the Bureau of Indian Affairs. These are the Association’s own public historical descriptions. They locate a particular community within the broader Tlingit world without treating the Association as the whole Tlingit people.

Read the sources [1] Douglas Indian Association

02

Displacement and renewed organizing

The booklet states that the City of Douglas burned Douglas Indian Village in 1962, destroying homes and belongings and dispersing residents. It describes the consequences as forced relocation and places renewed efforts to reassemble and rebuild tribal governance in the mid-1970s. This is a concise account of the Tribe’s historical interpretation and experience. Further archival and first-person reading is needed to follow particular families, official decisions and the longer course of rebuilding.

Read the sources [1] Douglas Indian Association

03

Environmental work for future generations

The Environmental Department frames a clean environment on land and sea and continuity of community lifeways as responsibilities to future generations. Its public page describes an Indian General Assistance Program and a Brownfield Tribal Response Program. It also reports soil and tissue sampling projects investigating contamination associated with historical mining in the Juneau–Douglas area. These descriptions show a community environmental agenda and reported research activity. They do not establish the safety of a place or food, prove contamination outcomes, or demonstrate that cleanup is complete.

Tribal government historyDouglas Indian AssociationSource 1

The A’akw Kwáan & T’aaku Kwáan: Douglas Indian Association Tribal History ↗

Publication: 2017-07-21 revision indicated in filename; printed booklet undated

A tribal account of regional roots, Douglas Indian Village, the 1962 burning and later rebuilding of governance.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Selected complete printed pp.1–4 (PDF pp.2–5), headings Background and Tribal History through the 1962 burning account. Text read; printed pp.3–4 also rendered locally and visually inspected. Cover metadata inspected. Later cemetery, ceremony, territory-map and fisheries-permit sections were not used.

Review recorded: November 2, 2026

Access note: Official tribal storage-hosted PDF downloaded. The same booklet on the land-trust site was identified as a duplicate and not counted separately. Existing recognition evidence is preserved; the booklet’s recognition chronology is not adopted as a new legal analysis.
